The first step in the process of taking an idea from concept to reality is to define the unmet
need.
Addressing the unmet need may serve to
Improve patient outcomes
Reduce variability in patient outcomes
Improve patient safety
Reduce economic cost
Increase efficiency
After the need is clearly identified, the inventor or product development team can brainstorm
the possible ways in which that need may be met.
If a potential solution to the need is identified and approved, the idea can be fleshed out
further via prototypes, drawings, and models.
Prototypes can be further evaluated via simulated-use testing, cadaver model studies,
laboratory studies, engineering testing, or hands-on evaluation from the orthopaedic surgeons
who would be the likely users of the device.
At every step, feedback will spur changes and new ideas on how to improve or modify the
device.
This process is iterative and helps ensure that the idea best serves its purpose in the market.
The product development team needs to recognize technology transfer, in which creators of a
technology seek a practical application for an already existing invention (ie, trying to find a
problem that requires a solution that already exists).
Formally Defining the Product
With a well-vetted concept in hand, the next step in the development process is to formally
define the product by creating a target product profile (TPP).
A well-constructed TPP should include the following components.
Clinical purpose and intended benefit
Target patient population
Intended use
Composition and configuration
Product performance attributes
Proposed labeling statements and claims
Manufacturing considerations
Storage, handling, shipping, and other environmental requirements

Commercial objectives, such as pricing, revenue estimates, and anticipated launch dates
Not all aspects of the TPP may be known at the outset. The TPP is meant to be a dynamic
document that is continually updated as new information arises.
A fully completed TPP is a marker of a mature product.
Evaluating the Business Opportunity of the Product
After the TPP is completed or near completion, it is time to analyze the financial opportunity of
the device before committing additional resources to its development.
The purpose of developing a business plan for the product is to determine whether the market
size, demand, anticipated pricing, and potential revenue of the device justify the financial time,
cost, and risk associated with its development.
A thorough business plan should address the topics and questions listed in Table 1.
A key aspect to the viability of any device is its manufacturability, or the ability of the product,
in its current design, to be fabricated at commercial scale at a cost that can be supported by
the market.
Manufacturability is heavily influenced by several factors, including design complexity, quality
requirements, supply constraints, raw material costs, labor costs, and manufacturing
environment needs.

Seeking Patent Protection
The medical device industry is fiercely competitive and consists of a combination of large, well-
established market players and new, up-and-coming startup companies.
Securing a patent from the US Patent Office protects the device from being copied directly or
mimicked in a way that the design, intended use, and clinical benefit are the same.

Often, multiple patents, or a patent strategy, are necessary to fully protect an idea from
infringement by the competition.
A well-constructed patent portfolio is key to materializing a profitable future for a new device
or idea. Consider the following two examples.
In the early 2000s, Kyphon introduced an instrument set for performing kyphoplasty.
Because of the strength of the patent portfolio protecting the Kyphon balloon tamp system,
other much larger companies were unable to copy or mimic the Kyphon design. Eventually,
Kyphon was acquired by Medtronic for $4.2 billion.
In the early 2000s, KFx Medical developed a novel technology for soft-tissue fixation that was
adopted readily by shoulder surgeons performing rotator cuff repair. Other well-established
companies attempted to copy the KFx Medical design but were prevented from doing so
because of KFx Medical’s robust patent portfolio. Consequently, KFx entered into license
agreements with multiple major orthopaedic implant companies, including Smith & Nephew,
Mitek/J&J, CONMED, Wright Medical, and Zimmer Biomet.
Designing Preclinical Studies
Any new implantable device requires testing in preclinical studies or animal models to
establish safety and efficacy.
The FDA typically requires that such studies be conducted under good laboratory practices
(GLPs) to ensure that the data produced by the studies are of high quality.
Performing studies under GLPs is expensive and typically lies beyond the capabilities of a
typical university environment. Therefore, most preclinical studies designed to support
regulatory submissions are performed by third-party contract laboratories that have the
infrastructure necessary to adhere to GLP requirements.
The tenets of GLP includes several factors.
Use of properly qualified personnel to conduct studies
Establishment of a study director to oversee research and ensure quality
Appropriate facilities for the care, feeding, and housing of animals
Provisions for equipment maintenance and calibration
Standard operating procedures to document all procedure and test methods
Provisions to ensure test articles are properly stored and handled
Identification of test facilities, equipment, materials, and reagents
Development of a protocol, testing plan, and reporting methodology
Provisions for archiving records and test data

Defining Success: Academia Versus Industry
Academia and industry define success differently with regard to product development (Figure
1).
In academia, a successful product development pathway typically ends with a first-in-man
clinical trial that demonstrates efficacy.
In industry, a successful product development pathway ends with a product that is approved
by the FDA, is covered by insurance companies, and is in demand by patients and providers,
all of which yield a profitable product.
Figure 1 Chart shows the academic and industrial foundations of product development. The
top panel illustrates a typical academic hierarchy of success, which begins with the design of a
therapy and ends with its first use in humans. In comparison, the industrial model (lower
panel) is designed upside-down, illustrating that early human data are considered in the
beginning of many product development efforts. Performance of a series of clinical studies
and subsequent FDA approval are necessary to apply for the reimbursement required for a
successful market launch. GMP = good manufacturing process, IND = investigational new drug.

Navigating the FDA Approval Process
The Role and Structure of the FDA
The purpose of the FDA is to protect public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, quality,
and security of human and veterinary drugs, biologics, vaccines, and medical devices.
The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act established the basic laws governing the
development of drugs and medical devices.
The Public Health Service Act established the basic laws governing biologic products.
New medical products fall under the regulatory scope of the Office of Medical Products,
Tobacco, and Specialty Laboratory Operations, which is divided into three centers.
Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, which is responsible for managing over-the-
counter and prescription drugs, including biologic therapeutics, such as monoclonal antibody
drugs, and generic drugs
Center for Devices and Radiological Health, which is responsible for overseeing medical
devices and radiation-emitting products
Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, which is responsible for managing biologic and
related products
Determining whether a new product will be classified as a drug, a device, or a biologic is critical
in determining the feasibility of receiving FDA approval and successfully launching the product
because each designation carries a different level of quality standards and evidence required
for approval.
To determine the category in which the product will be classified, the intended use and
suspected mode of action by which the product achieves its purpose must be defined (Table
2).

Orthobiologics are particularly challenging because they may be exempt from FDA
premarket authorization if the biologic meets very specific criteria (Figure 2). If it does not,
the product must have premarket FDA approval, which is a long and arduous process.
Examples of orthobiologics that have been subject to FDA approval include culture-
expanded chondrocytes for cartilage repair, manipulated amniotic membrane for
inflammatory modulation, and purified stem cell preparation from any tissue source.

Through the FDA: Clearance or Approval?
If a medical product is to be marketed legally in the US, it must be cleared or approved by the
FDA.
Cleared refers to devices that have used the 510(k) Premarket Notification Process and have
been deemed similar enough to another legally marketed device to allow for their sale in the
United States without additional regulatory hurdles.
Approved refers to products that have gone through the Premarket Approval (PMA) or
Biological License Application (BLA) process and have been deemed safe and effective for their
intended use.
The Presubmission Process
The presubmission process is a voluntary program coordinated by the FDA that allows would-
be applicants to obtain feedback and advice from the FDA before formally submitting an
Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) or a marketing application (eg, PMA, 510(k), or BLA).
Participation in the presubmission program allows the FDA to become familiar with the new
product early in the process so that potentially insurmountable hurdles to approval can be
identified before additional resources are invested in the product development and approval
process.
The FDA provides feedback within 75 to 90 days of submission.
Determining Which Marketing Application to Submit
Determining which marketing application to submit to the FDA depends on the risk attributed
to the device.
Devices are classified as class I, class II, or class III, with higher classification indicating greater
risk.
The risk-based classification system depends on the intended use of the device and its
indications for use and the level of control necessary to ensure adequate safety.
Class I devices are exempt from premarket notification.
Class II devices usually require 510(k) clearance.
Class III devices, which are associated with the highest risk, require an IDE, clinical studies, and
PMA.
Table 3 lists examples of devices that have been categorized into each class.

A 510(k) submission contains detailed technical, safety, and performance information about
the device, which demonstrates that the device is at least as safe and effective (ie, substantially
equivalent) to a legally marketed device.
Typically, the 510(k) pathway requires only bench testing, logic, and/or animal data rather than
clinical evidence, making it much cheaper and quicker to bring a product to market.
IDE and PMA Pathway
The IDE/PMA pathway is the FDA’s process of scientific and regulatory review reserved for class
III (highest risk) device safety and effectiveness.
This process has the most stringent device-marketing application.
Given the high risk associated with class III devices, this pathway typically includes animal
studies, nonclinical in vitro studies, and well-controlled clinical investigations.
An IDE is required for the unapproved device to be used in a clinical investigation setting.
The IDE requires that
The device sponsor (applicant) demonstrate that substantial preclinical evidence exists to
support the belief that the risks posed to human subjects associated with the use of the
investigational device are outweighed by the anticipated benefits.
The proposed investigation is scientifically sound.
The full PMA application includes technical information consisting of details about the
manufacturing of the device, nonclinical laboratory studies, and clinical investigations.
The FDA performs an initial, in-depth review of the scientific, regulatory, and quality data
provided by the sponsor.
Then, technical evidence is reviewed by an advisory panel of independent experts.
The FDA may request preapproval inspection of the manufacturer.
Approval also may include requirements for post-approval studies.
The timeline from PMA submission to final determination often takes more than 1 year.
Investigational New Drug/BLA Pathway
Products classified as biologic go through a process that is similar in structure to the IDE/PMA
pathway.
Similar to the IDE/PMA pathway, the investigational new drug/BLA pathway requires
submission of product manufacturing and technical information, preclinical studies, and well-
controlled clinical investigations.

Similar to the IDE/PMA pathway, sponsors of the unapproved biologic or drug product must
first submit an investigational new drug application that provides evidence demonstrating a
reason to believe the proposed biologic or drug will provide a benefit that outweighs the risks
associated with its use.
The most notable orthopaedic example of a biologic that successfully navigated the
investigational new drug/BLA pathway is culture-expanded cartilage repair products, which
took more than 10 years to gain approval.

Life After the FDA: A Financially Successful Product
Crucial to Product Success: A Reliable Payment Source
If a new product is to be financially successful after receiving FDA clearance or approval, it
must be in demand.

If a physician, group or hospital system is to be willing to use a new product or device, they
must first know that they will be reimbursed for the cost of the product or that it is so
inexpensive that it will not affect the bottom line. The latter rarely occurs with new devices.
For reimbursement (typically from a third-party insurer) to occur, the new product or device
must be assigned a common procedural terminology (CPT) code.
For many new devices cleared through the 510(k) pathway, a CPT code already exists.
However, novel devices may require a new code.
The American Medical Association maintains the physician CPT codes.
The AAOS Coding Coverage and Reimbursement Committee acts as an adjunct to the
American Medical Association and oversees the codes relevant to orthopaedic surgery.
Creating a new code typically requires clinical evidence of efficacy and evidence of
substantial use, meaning that many physicians are incorporating the new procedure into
their practice.
Tables 4 and 5 provide the amount and quality of evidence required by the American
Medical Association before a new CPT code is considered.
Without a CPT code, providers have no way to seek reimbursement for the new product
from the payee, typically an insurance company.
After a CPT code is associated with the new device, hospitals or physician groups and
insurance companies agree to payment rates for the CPT code.
Providers then determine whether the reimbursement rate associated with the CPT code
justifies the use of the new product or device. Most often, too low a reimbursement makes
the use of new devices or products cost prohibitive for the hospital.
Even if a new device has an associated CPT code and is not financially cost prohibitive to
providers or hospital systems, insurance companies may not cover the procedure or the
implant if the insurer does not feel that evidence exists to support the procedure or the use
of the device.
Each insurer determines what CPT codes it will or will not reimburse.
These decisions typically are predetermined, but appeals can be made to the insurer if
the physician feels it is appropriate
The most successful devices are those that are associated with CPT codes (either pre-
existing codes or those created for use with the new device), have adequate demand, and
are covered by most or all large insurers.
